claim: Nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) are composed of ~30 proteins termed nucleoporins or Nups.
source: Highly conserved across all eukaryotes, NPCs are composed of ~30 proteins, termed nucleoporins or Nups, which can be placed into two general categories.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the composition of NPCs.

claim: FG-Nups line the NPC channel and directly facilitate the movement of nuclear transport factors and their cargoes through the NPC.
source: Among its functions, the core scaffold acts as a binding surface for a second set of Nups (FG-Nups) that line the NPC channel and directly facilitate the movement of nuclear transport factors and their cargoes through the NPC (Field et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Field et al., 2014.

claim: Various FG-Nups have been detected in the nucleoplasm and have been shown to move between intranuclear sites and NPCs.
source: For example, various FG-Nups have been detected in the nucleoplasm, which have been shown to move between intranuclear sites and NPCs (Rabut et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rabut et al., 2004.

claim: Intranuclear Nups have been reported to regulate gene expression through binding transcription sites.
source: In addition to contributing to nuclear transport (Sakiyama et al., 2016; Zahn et al., 2016), these intranuclear Nups have been reported to regulate gene expression through binding transcription sites (Capelson et al., 2010; Kalverda et al., 2010; Ptak et al., 2014), including immune response genes (Faria et al., 2006; Light et al., 2013; Panda et al., 2014), and influencing chromatin organization (Kalverda and Fornerod, 2010; Liang and Hetzer, 2011; Ptak and Wozniak, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Nup98 is visible throughout the nucleoplasm and can accumulate at intranuclear structures termed GLFG bodies.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis revealed that Nup98 is visible throughout the nucleoplasm, but can accumulate at intranuclear structures termed GLFG bodies (Griffis et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Griffis et al., 2002.

claim: The mobility of NPC-associated and nucleoplasmic Nup98 is dependent on ongoing transcription in the cell.
source: Further, the mobility of NPC-associated and nucleoplasmic Nup98 is dependent on ongoing transcription in the cell (Griffis et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Griffis et al., 2002.

claim: In Drosophila, Nup98 associates with actively transcribed genes, especially those involved in development and cell cycle regulation.
source: Studies in Drosophila revealed the association of Nup98 with actively transcribed genes, especially those involved in development and cell cycle regulation, with modulation of cellular Nup98 levels (over-expression or knock-down) altering transcription of these genes (Capelson et al., 2010; Kalverda et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Capelson et al., 2010 and Kalverda et al., 2010.

claim: In mammalian cells, Nup98 associates with chromatin and regulates gene expression during the differentiation of embryonic stem cells into neural progenitor cells.
source: Similarly, in mammalian cells, Nup98 has been shown to associate with chromatin and regulate gene expression during the differentiation of embryonic stem cells into neural progenitor cells (Liang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liang et al., 2013.

claim: Mammalian Nup98 binds to HLA-DRA, an interferon-ɣ induced gene exhibiting transcriptional memory.
source: Light and colleagues showed that mammalian Nup98 binds to HLA-DRA (Light et al., 2013), an interferon-ɣ induced gene exhibiting transcriptional memory (i.e. a gene that displays rapid induction given a recent history of being activated).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Light et al., 2013.

claim: In the absence of Nup98, transcriptional memory of HLA-DRA was lost and the binding of RNA polymerase II at promoters poised for reactivation was reduced.
source: In the absence of Nup98, transcriptional memory was lost and the binding of RNA polymerase II at promoters poised for reactivation was reduced, which matched similar findings in yeast (Light et al., 2010, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Light et al., 2010 and 2013.

claim: In Drosophila, Nup98 binds to the promoter regions of certain active genes and is required for their transcription.
source: In Drosophila, Pascual-Garcia and colleagues showed binding of Nup98 to the promoter regions of certain active genes and a requirement for Nup98 in their transcription (Pascual-Garcia et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pascual-Garcia et al., 2014.

claim: Nup98 binding to genes in Drosophila was dependent on TRX and MBD-R2, a component of the NSL complex that directs histone H4K16 acetylation.
source: Nup98 binding to these genes was dependent on TRX and MBD-R2, a component of the NSL (nonspecific lethal) complex that directs histone H4K16 acetylation.
evidence: This is a statement from the manuscript describing findings from Pascual-Garcia et al., 2014.

claim: The loss of Nup98 did not change H4K16 acetylation or TRX-mediated H3K4 trimethylation patterns in Drosophila.
source: However, the loss of Nup98 did not change H4K16 acetylation or TRX-mediated H3K4 trimethylation patterns, both of which are required for active transcription and transcriptional memory.
evidence: This is a statement from the manuscript describing findings from Pascual-Garcia et al., 2014.

claim: More than twenty-eight different chromosomal rearrangements involving the NUP98 gene have been identified in hematopoietic malignancies.
source: More evidence for the role of Nup98 in gene expression regulation comes from studies of hematopoietic malignancies. More than twenty-eight different chromosomal rearrangements involving the NUP98 gene have been identified.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: Nup98 fusion proteins have been shown to alter transcription through fusing the N-terminal domain of Nup98 to a C-terminal domain that usually contains a chromatin/DNA interacting region.
source: The resulting fusion proteins have been shown to alter transcription through fusing the N-terminal domain of Nup98 (Bai et al., 2006; Kasper et al., 1999) to a C-terminal domain that usually contains a chromatin/DNA interacting region (Capitanio and Wozniak, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bai et al., 2006, Kasper et al., 1999, and Capitanio and Wozniak, 2012.

claim: The oncogenicity of several Nup98 fusions has been demonstrated in mouse models where Nup98 fusions lead to acute myeloid leukemia recapitulating the human disease phenotype.
source: The oncogenicity of several Nup98 fusions has been demonstrated in mouse models where Nup98 fusions lead to acute myeloid leukemia recapitulating the human disease phenotype (Gough et al., 2011; Moore et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gough et al., 2011 and Moore et al., 2007.

claim: Nup98 associates with the p21 mRNA 3'UTR preventing degradation by the exosome.
source: A recent publication reported that Nup98 associates with the p21 mRNA 3'UTR preventing degradation by the exosome, with several other putative target mRNAs being similarly regulated (Singer et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Singer et al., 2012.

claim: GFP-NUP98 immunoprecipitation from HEK293T cells identified previously characterized Nup98 interactors such as Nup88, Rae1, NXF1, and CRM1.
source: Mass spectrometry (MS) analysis of purified protein complexes (Figure 1, Supplementary file 1A) identified previously characterized Nup98 interactors, such as Nup88 (Griffis et al., 2003), Rae1 (Pritchard et al., 1999), NXF1 (Bachi et al., 2000), and CRM1 (Oka et al., 2010), as well as several other proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from mass spectrometry analysis and citations to previous studies.

claim: Nup98-interacting proteins function in specific mRNA metabolism events including mRNA processing, splicing, stabilization, and transport.
source: Enrichment analysis based on Gene Ontology (GO) annotations indeed showed that these sets of GFP-Nup98 interacting proteins function in specific mRNA metabolism events including mRNA processing, splicing, stabilization, and transport (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis of the protein-protein interaction network shown in Figure 2A.

claim: DHX9 and hnRNP U were selected for further analysis based on their abundance in the GFP-Nup98 immunoprecipitation and the number of protein-protein interactions within the network.
source: Therefore, we selected Nup98 interactors for further study on the basis of abundance in the GFP-Nup98 immunoprecipitation (IP) and the number of PPIs occurring with the other proteins within the network (Figure 2A and B). Based on these features, DHX9 and hnRNP U were selected for further analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The association of both DHX9 and hnRNP U with Nup98 was confirmed by reciprocal immunoprecipitations of endogenous Nup98, DHX9, and hnRNP U.
source: Importantly, the association of both DHX9 and hnRNP U with Nup98 was confirmed by reciprocal immunoprecipitations of endogenous Nup98, DHX9, and hnRNP U (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: DHX9 and hnRNP U are broadly distributed within the nucleoplasm in a punctate pattern and appear excluded from nucleoli.
source: Similar to previous reports (Uhlen et al., 2010; Uhlén et al., 2015), DHX9 and hnRNP U were broadly distributed within the nucleoplasm in a punctate pattern, but appeared excluded from nucleoli.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3 and citations to previous reports.

claim: Neither DHX9 nor hnRNP U appeared concentrated at the nuclear envelope.
source: Neither protein appeared concentrated at the NE (Figure 3, inset).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Depletion of Nup98 resulted in no detectable changes in the distribution pattern of hnRNP U.
source: Depletion of Nup98 resulted in no detectable changes in the distribution pattern of hnRNP U (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The loss of Nup98 caused the appearance of bright DHX9 foci in the nucleoplasm.
source: However, the loss of Nup98 caused the appearance of bright DHX9 foci in the nucleoplasm.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The exclusion of DHX9 from nucleoli observed in mock-treated cells was less pronounced in Nup98-depleted cells.
source: Moreover, the exclusion of DHX9 from nucleoli observed in mock-treated cells was less pronounced in Nup98-depleted cells, suggesting that DHX9 has greater access to the nucleolus in the absence of Nup98.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4 and inference from the observation.

claim: Depletion of DHX9 did not noticeably alter Nup98 localization.
source: In contrast, depletion of DHX9 (or hnRNP U; data not shown) did not noticeably alter Nup98 localization (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Elevated levels of Nup98 accumulate in intranuclear foci termed GLFG-bodies.
source: Elevated levels of Nup98 accumulate in intranuclear foci termed GLFG-bodies (Griffis et al., 2002), and we observed the formation of these foci in cells producing GFP-Nup98 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and a citation to Griffis et al., 2002.

claim: DHX9 was recruited to the GFP-Nup98 foci.
source: Importantly, DHX9 was recruited to the GFP-Nup98 foci.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: No visible impact on hnRNP U distribution was observed in GFP-Nup98 producing cells.
source: By contrast, no visible impact on hnRNP U distribution was observed in GFP-Nup98 producing cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The change in DHX9 distribution upon GFP-Nup98 expression was not accompanied by alterations in the cellular levels of DHX9.
source: The change in DHX9 distribution was not accompanied by alterations in the cellular levels of DHX9 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), thus the DHX9 associated with GFP-Nup98 foci was likely recruited from other locations.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and inference from the observation.

claim: DHX9 was primarily present in a nucleoplasmic fraction, while Nup98 was detected in both the nucleoplasmic and NE fractions.
source: Consistent with localization data, DHX9 was primarily present in a nucleoplasmic fraction, while Nup98 was detected in both the nucleoplasmic and NE fractions, which were further validated with antibodies against other NE and nucleoplasmic proteins (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by nuclear fractionation and western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: DHX9 was only detected in association with nucleoplasmic Nup98, although similar amounts of Nup98 were purified from both nucleoplasmic and NE fractions.
source: Immunoprecipitations from these fractions showed that DHX9 was only detected in association with nucleoplasmic Nup98, although similar amounts of Nup98 were purified from both fractions, and that nucleoplasmic DHX9 was able to immunopurify Nup98 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The Nup98-DHX9 complex is primarily present in the nucleoplasm.
source: Cumulatively, these results strongly argue that the Nup98-DHX9 complex is primarily present in the nucleoplasm, and that the N-terminal FG/GLFG domain of Nup98 interacts with DHX9.
evidence: This claim is inferred from multiple experimental results including fractionation, immunoprecipitation, and immunofluorescence data.

claim: The N-terminal FG/GLFG domain of Nup98 interacts with DHX9.
source: Cumulatively, these results strongly argue that the Nup98-DHX9 complex is primarily present in the nucleoplasm, and that the N-terminal FG/GLFG domain of Nup98 interacts with DHX9.
evidence: This claim is inferred from multiple experimental results including immunoprecipitation data with Nup98 truncations.

claim: When parallel samples of bead-bound Nup98 complexes were incubated with RNase A, levels of Nup98-associated DHX9 were reduced, while PRKDC and associated Nups were unaffected.
source: However, when parallel samples of bead-bound complexes were incubated with RNase A in amounts sufficient to degrade all detectable RNA (Höck et al., 2007; Moore et al., 2014; Ule et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2008), levels of Nup98-associated DHX9 were reduced, while PRKDC and associated Nups were unaffected.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: RNA, directly or indirectly, contributes to the interaction of Nup98 with DHX9.
source: These results imply that RNA, directly or indirectly, contributes to the interaction of Nup98 with DHX9.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that RNase A treatment reduces DHX9 binding to Nup98.

claim: Recombinant Nup98 and DHX9 can interact in vitro.
source: To extend our characterization of the in vivo interactions between Nup98, DHX9, and RNA, we examined whether recombinant Nup98 and DHX9 could interact using in vitro binding assays. Magnetic beads coupled to anti-DHX9 antibodies were incubated with GST-DHX9. GST alone or GST-Nup98 was then added to bead-bound GST-DHX9. Only the GST-Nup98 protein bound to the beads, suggesting a direct interaction between DHX9 and Nup98. (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The interaction of untagged or GST-tagged DHX9 with Nup98 was partially reduced by the addition of RNase A.
source: Binding reactions conducted under these conditions reveal that the interaction of untagged or GST-tagged DHX9 with Nup98 was partially reduced by the addition of RNase A, while the addition of RNA (poly I:C) did not appear to alter the binding of DHX9 to Nup98 (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The addition of RNA (poly I:C) did not appear to alter the binding of DHX9 to Nup98 in vitro.
source: Binding reactions conducted under these conditions reveal that the interaction of untagged or GST-tagged DHX9 with Nup98 was partially reduced by the addition of RNase A, while the addition of RNA (poly I:C) did not appear to alter the binding of DHX9 to Nup98 (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Using the bead halo assay, binding of recombinant Nup98 to DHX9 was detected and quantified.
source: Using this assay, we detected and quantified the binding of recombinant Nup98 to DHX9 (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), and again the addition of RNA did not significantly alter the relative strength of this interaction, but the inclusion of RNase A reduced the level of DHX9 binding to Nup98 (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by bead halo assay data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The addition of RNA did not significantly alter the relative strength of the Nup98-DHX9 interaction in the bead halo assay, but the inclusion of RNase A reduced the level of DHX9 binding to Nup98.
source: Using this assay, we detected and quantified the binding of recombinant Nup98 to DHX9 (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), and again the addition of RNA did not significantly alter the relative strength of this interaction, but the inclusion of RNase A reduced the level of DHX9 binding to Nup98 (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by bead halo assay data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: An N-terminal region of DHX9 (residues 1–380), containing two double-stranded RNA binding motifs (DRBM1 and DRBM2), bound to Nup98.
source: We observed that an N-terminal region (residues 1–380), containing two double-stranded RNA binding motifs (DRBM1 and DRBM2), and a C-terminal segment (residues 821–1270), containing an (OB)-binding fold and a single-stranded RNA-binding RGG-box, bound to Nup98.
evidence: This claim is supported by bead halo assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: A C-terminal segment of DHX9 (residues 821–1270), containing an (OB)-binding fold and a single-stranded RNA-binding RGG-box, bound to Nup98.
source: We observed that an N-terminal region (residues 1–380), containing two double-stranded RNA binding motifs (DRBM1 and DRBM2), and a C-terminal segment (residues 821–1270), containing an (OB)-binding fold and a single-stranded RNA-binding RGG-box, bound to Nup98.
evidence: This claim is supported by bead halo assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: DHX9's central region (residues 381–820), containing its ATP-dependent helicase domain, did not bind GST-Nup98 under these conditions.
source: Conversely, DHX9's central region (residues 381–820), containing its ATP-dependent helicase domain (Zhang and Grosse, 1997), did not bind GST-Nup98 under these conditions (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by bead halo assay data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The interactions of the N- and C-terminal domains of DHX9-GFP with GST-Nup98 appeared to be facilitated by the presence of RNA, as these interactions were sensitive to RNase A.
source: The interactions of the N- and C-terminal domains of DHX9-GFP with GST-Nup98 appeared to be facilitated by the presence of RNA, as these interactions were sensitive to RNase A.
evidence: This claim is supported by bead halo assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The addition of RNA (poly I:C) prior to mixing of the two proteins stimulated binding of GST-Nup98 and the N-terminal domain of DHX9-GFP.
source: Furthermore, the addition of RNA (poly I:C) prior to mixing of the two proteins stimulated binding of GST-Nup98 and the N-terminal domain of DHX9-GFP (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by bead halo assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: DHX9 can directly bind Nup98 and their association is augmented by RNA.
source: Cumulatively, these data lead us to conclude that DHX9 can directly bind Nup98 and that their association is augmented by RNA.
evidence: This claim is inferred from multiple in vitro binding assay results.

claim: The DHX9-Nup98 interaction is likely mediated by the N- and C-terminal domains of DHX9.
source: The DHX9-Nup98 interaction is likely mediated by the N- and C-terminal domains of DHX9.
evidence: This claim is inferred from bead halo assay data showing that these domains bind Nup98.

claim: A basal ATPase rate for recombinant DHX9 was observed that was stimulated by the addition of RNA to levels comparable to that previously reported for DHX9.
source: We observed a basal ATPase rate for recombinant DHX9 that was stimulated by the addition of RNA to levels comparable to that previously reported for DHX9 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) (Schütz et al., 2010; Zhang and Grosse, 1994; 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATPase assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and citations to previous studies.

claim: In the presence of excess RNA (poly I:C), the addition of GST-Nup98 induced a dose-dependent increase in GST-DHX9 ATPase activity reaching levels approximately five-fold higher than GST-DHX9 and RNA alone at the highest GST-Nup98 concentration tested.
source: In the presence of excess RNA (poly I:C), the addition of GST-Nup98 induced a dose-dependent increase in GST-DHX9 ATPase activity reaching levels approximately five-fold higher than GST-DHX9 and RNA alone at the highest GST-Nup98 concentration tested (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATPase assay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: A similar level of stimulation of DHX9 ATPase activity was also observed using untagged versions of DHX9 and Nup98.
source: A similar level of stimulation was also observed using untagged versions of DHX9 and Nup98 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATPase assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DHX9 ATPase activity was increased upon addition of the N-terminal FG/GLFG domain of Nup98.
source: DHX9 ATPase activity was also increased upon addition of the N-terminal FG/GLFG domain of Nup98.
evidence: This claim is supported by ATPase assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Neither the C-terminal domain of Nup98 or GST alone caused significant changes in DHX9 ATPase activity.
source: By contrast, neither the C-terminal domain of Nup98 or GST alone caused significant changes in DHX9 ATPase activity, nor could GST-Nup98 stimulate GST-DHX9 in the absence of RNA (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATPase assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: GST-Nup98 could not stimulate GST-DHX9 in the absence of RNA.
source: By contrast, neither the C-terminal domain of Nup98 or GST alone caused significant changes in DHX9 ATPase activity, nor could GST-Nup98 stimulate GST-DHX9 in the absence of RNA (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATPase assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Nup98 functions as a positive regulator of DHX9 ATPase activity in the context of RNA.
source: These data indicate that Nup98 functions as a positive regulator of DHX9 ATPase activity in the context of RNA.
evidence: This claim is inferred from ATPase assay data showing that Nup98 stimulates DHX9 ATPase activity in the presence of RNA.

claim: There is a statistically significant overlap in mRNA binding datasets for Nup98 and DHX9, with ~37% of the Nup98-interacting mRNAs also detected bound to DHX9 and ~40% of the DHX9 bound transcripts interacting with Nup98 (p=2.5×10−93).
source: We find a statistically significant overlap in these datasets with ~37% of the Nup98-interacting mRNAs also detected bound to DHX9 and ~40% of the DHX9 bound transcripts interacting with Nup98 (p=2.5×10−93; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of published mRNA binding datasets for Nup98 and DHX9.

claim: JunD, Myc, FoxP2, HoxA2, and ZFY encoding mRNAs were detected bound to both DHX9 and Nup98.
source: As anticipated, JunD, Myc, FoxP2, HoxA2, and ZFY encoding mRNAs were detected bound to both DHX9 and Nup98 (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Both NHLH2 and HEXIM1 showed no interaction with either DHX9 or Nup98.
source: By contrast, both NHLH2 and HEXIM1, showed no interaction with either DHX9 or Nup98.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Both Nup98 and DHX9 interacted with the Adenovirus early region 1A (E1A) encoding RNA.
source: Both Nup98 and DHX9 also interacted with the Adenovirus early region 1A (E1A) encoding RNA, a well known splicing reporter whose metabolism is regulated by several hnRNPs and RNA helicases (Zheng, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 8 and a citation to Zheng, 2010.

claim: Nup98 and DHX9 interact with, and potentially regulate, a shared set of mRNAs in vivo.
source: These results suggest that Nup98 and DHX9 interact with, and potentially regulate, a shared set of mRNAs in vivo.
evidence: This claim is inferred from RNA immunoprecipitation and RT-PCR data showing that Nup98 and DHX9 bind similar mRNAs.

claim: Upon depletion of DHX9, five of six mRNAs (E1A, FOXP2, HOXA2, MYC and ZFY) showed a significant decrease in Nup98 association relative to the input as compared to mock-depleted cells.
source: As shown in Figure 9, upon depletion of DHX9, five of six mRNAs (E1A, FOXP2, HOXA2, MYC and ZFY) showed a significant decrease in Nup98 association relative to the input as compared to mock-depleted cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation and qPCR data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Depletion of Nup98 led to a significant increase in the amount of each of the six mRNAs bound to DHX9.
source: By contrast, depletion of Nup98 led to a significant increase in the amount of each of the six mRNAs bound to DHX9.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation and qPCR data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The changes in the association of Nup98 or DHX9 with these mRNAs does not appear to be due to a change in the nuclear export status of the tested mRNAs.
source: The changes in the association of Nup98 or DHX9 with these mRNAs does not appear to be due to a change in the nuclear export status of the tested mRNAs (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by nuclear/cytoplasmic fractionation and qPCR data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nup98 and DHX9 influence each others association with mRNA.
source: These results show that Nup98 and DHX9 influence each others association with mRNA, and are consistent with a model in which DHX9 promotes the association of Nup98 with specific mRNAs, and Nup98 facilitates the release of these mRNAs from DHX9.
evidence: This claim is inferred from RNA immunoprecipitation and qPCR data showing interdependent mRNA binding.

claim: DHX9 promotes the association of Nup98 with specific mRNAs.
source: These results show that Nup98 and DHX9 influence each others association with mRNA, and are consistent with a model in which DHX9 promotes the association of Nup98 with specific mRNAs, and Nup98 facilitates the release of these mRNAs from DHX9.
evidence: This claim is inferred from RNA immunoprecipitation and qPCR data showing that DHX9 depletion reduces Nup98 binding to mRNAs.

claim: Nup98 facilitates the release of mRNAs from DHX9.
source: These results show that Nup98 and DHX9 influence each others association with mRNA, and are consistent with a model in which DHX9 promotes the association of Nup98 with specific mRNAs, and Nup98 facilitates the release of these mRNAs from DHX9.
evidence: This claim is inferred from RNA immunoprecipitation and qPCR data showing that Nup98 depletion increases DHX9 binding to mRNAs.

claim: Both Nup98 and DHX9 mapped to the six gene loci whose transcripts were bound to Nup98 and DHX9.
source: As shown in Figure 10, both Nup98 and DHX9 mapped to the six gene loci whose transcripts were bound to Nup98 and DHX9.
evidence: This claim is supported by DamID and qPCR data shown in Figure 10.

claim: For JUND and MYC, both Nup98 and DHX9 showed robust binding to the 5' promoter regions of these genes, while binding to regions within their ORFs were lower or absent.
source: For JUND and MYC, two regions within these genes were examined: a 5' region containing the promoter and a region within the 3' half of the ORF. For both Nup98 and DHX9, robust binding was detected to the 5' promoter regions of these genes, while binding to regions within their ORFs were lower or absent.
evidence: This claim is supported by DamID and qPCR data shown in Figure 10.

claim: No detectable binding of Nup98 or DHX9 was observed to the NHLH2 and HEXIM1 genes.
source: Similarly, no detectable binding was observed to the NHLH2 and HEXIM1 genes, consistent with our observation that the transcripts from these genes were not detected in association with Nup98 and DHX9 (Figure 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by DamID and qPCR data shown in Figure 10.

claim: The binding of Nup98 and DHX9 to the gene loci tested was interdependent on one another.
source: The binding of Nup98 and DHX9 to the gene loci tested was also interdependent on one another. Depletion of Nup98 or DHX9 significantly reduced the interactions of its binding partner with the target gene (Figure 10 and Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by DamID and qPCR data shown in Figure 10 and Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Nup98-DHX9 complex binds to specific genes and their transcripts.
source: We therefore suggest that the Nup98-DHX9 complex binds to specific genes and their transcripts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from DamID and RNA immunoprecipitation data showing that Nup98 and DHX9 bind to the same gene loci and their transcripts.

claim: Expression of exogenous DHX9 in cells containing the CRE-luciferase reporter increased production of luciferase.
source: Similar to previous reports, expression of exogenous DHX9 in cells containing the CRE-luciferase reporter increased production of luciferase (Figure 12).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 12.

claim: In the absence of exogenous DHX9, expression of Nup98 had no significant effect on the expression of luciferase.
source: In the absence of exogenous DHX9, expression of Nup98 had no significant effect on the expression of luciferase.
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 12.

claim: The stimulatory effect of Nup98 binding to DHX9 supports its role in transcription.
source: These results are consistent with our in vitro observations showing Nup98 can stimulate the ATPase activity of DHX9, and they suggest that the stimulatory effect of Nup98 binding to DHX9 supports its role in transcription.
evidence: This claim is inferred from luciferase reporter assay data and ATPase assay data.

claim: The specific genes detected bound to Nup98 and DHX9 exhibited altered transcript levels upon depletion of these proteins.
source: Consistent with these data, the specific genes we detected bound to Nup98 and DHX9 exhibited altered transcript levels upon depletion of these proteins (Figure 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 11.

claim: Analysis of RNA-Seq data revealed shared sets of genes with altered transcription upon depletion of Nup98 or DHX9.
source: Furthermore, analysis of RNA-Seq data (Chen et al., 2014; Franks et al., 2016) revealed shared sets of genes with altered transcription upon depletion of these proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of published RNA-Seq data.

claim: A comparison of RNA-Seq data sets shows significant overlap in the identity of gene products affected by the depletion of either Nup98 or DHX9 (287 genes with altered expression upon DHX9 or Nup98 depletion, p=3.24×10−36).
source: A comparison of these data sets shows significant overlap in the identity of gene products affected by the depletion of either protein (287 genes with altered expression upon DHX9 or Nup98 depletion, p=3.24×10−36; see Material and methods), consistent with the idea that these proteins form a functional complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: A significant number (p-value 2.38 × 10−4) of genes exhibiting altered expression upon Nup98 depletion contain a putative cAMP-response element (CRE).
source: Interestingly, a significant number (p-value 2.38 × 10−4) of those genes exhibiting altered expression upon Nup98 depletion contain a putative cAMP-response element (CRE) (Zhang et al., 2005), a regulatory element whose transcriptional activity can be regulated by DHX9 (Aratani et al., 2001; Fidaleo et al., 2016; Lee and Pelletier, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of RNA-Seq data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Depletion of Nup98 led to a 1.9 fold increase in pre-spliced isoform of the E1A transcript.
source: Depletion of Nup98 or DHX9 resulted in a 1.9 or 1.8 fold increase in pre-spliced isoform of the transcript (Figure 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 11 (though the figure reference appears to be Figure 13 based on context).

claim: Depletion of DHX9 resulted in a 1.8 fold increase in pre-spliced isoform of the E1A transcript.
source: Depletion of Nup98 or DHX9 resulted in a 1.9 or 1.8 fold increase in pre-spliced isoform of the transcript (Figure 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 11 (though the figure reference appears to be Figure 13 based on context).

claim: Depletion of Nup98 led to significantly increased levels of the 12S, 11S and 10S E1A isoforms.
source: Furthermore, we observed differential effects on the levels of the various splicing isoforms. Depletion of Nup98 led to significantly increased levels of the 12S, 11S and 10S isoforms.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 13.

claim: A similar increase in 12S and 11S E1A isoform was detected in cells depleted of DHX9.
source: A similar increase in 12S and 11S isoform was detected in cells depleted of DHX9.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 13.

claim: DHX9 depletion caused significant decreases in 9S and 13S E1A isoform abundance.
source: DHX9 depletion also caused significant decreases in 9S and 13S abundance.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 13.

claim: The interactions of Nup98 and DHX9 with specific mRNAs, such as E1A, regulates their splicing.
source: These results suggest that the interactions of Nup98 and DHX9 with specific mRNAs, such as E1A, regulates their splicing.
evidence: This claim is inferred from qPCR data showing altered E1A splicing isoforms upon Nup98 or DHX9 depletion.

claim: Intranuclear Nup98 functions as a regulator of DHX9.
source: In aggregate, our observations lead us to conclude that intranuclear Nup98 functions as a regulator of DHX9.
evidence: This is a summary claim inferred from multiple experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nup98 binds DHX9 in the nucleoplasm.
source: We have shown using a combination of in vitro and in vivo assays that Nup98 directly binds DHX9 in the nucleoplasm and this interaction is facilitated by RNA.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by multiple experimental results including fractionation, immunoprecipitation, and immunofluorescence data.

claim: The interaction between Nup98 and DHX9 is facilitated by RNA.
source: We have shown using a combination of in vitro and in vivo assays that Nup98 directly binds DHX9 in the nucleoplasm and this interaction is facilitated by RNA.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by multiple experimental results including RNase treatment and in vitro binding assays.

claim: Binding of Nup98 to DHX9 can stimulate the ATPase activity of DHX9.
source: Importantly, binding of Nup98 to DHX9 can stimulate the ATPase activity of DHX9 and support the role of this DExH/D-box protein in the transcription and splicing of a subset of genes.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by ATPase assay data.

claim: Binding of Nup98 to DHX9 supports the role of DHX9 in the transcription and splicing of a subset of genes.
source: Importantly, binding of Nup98 to DHX9 can stimulate the ATPase activity of DHX9 and support the role of this DExH/D-box protein in the transcription and splicing of a subset of genes.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by luciferase reporter assay data and splicing analysis.

claim: Nup98 and DHX9 bind to similar gene loci and mRNAs, and these interactions are interdependent upon one another.
source: Consistent with these observations, our analysis revealed that Nup98 and DHX9 bind to similar gene loci and mRNAs, and these interactions are interdependent upon one another.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by DamID and RNA immunoprecipitation data.

claim: DHX9 contains two double-stranded RNA binding domains (dsRBD) within the N-terminal third of the protein.
source: DHX9 contains two double-stranded RNA binding domains (dsRBD) within the N-terminal third of the protein (Zhang and Grosse, 1997), while the C-terminal third of the protein contains an oligonucleotide/oligosaccharide (OB)-binding fold and an RGG-box, a domain that characteristically binds single-stranded nucleic acids.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about DHX9 structure supported by a citation.

claim: The C-terminal third of DHX9 contains an oligonucleotide/oligosaccharide (OB)-binding fold and an RGG-box, a domain that characteristically binds single-stranded nucleic acids.
source: DHX9 contains two double-stranded RNA binding domains (dsRBD) within the N-terminal third of the protein (Zhang and Grosse, 1997), while the C-terminal third of the protein contains an oligonucleotide/oligosaccharide (OB)-binding fold and an RGG-box, a domain that characteristically binds single-stranded nucleic acids.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about DHX9 structure.

claim: The N- and C-terminal regions of DHX9 containing the dsRBDs and the RGG-box are thought to be spatially positioned in close proximity and contribute to the nucleic acid binding properties of DHX9.
source: The N- and C-terminal regions of DHX9 containing the dsRBDs and the RGG-box are thought to be spatially positioned in close proximity and contribute to the nucleic acid binding properties of DHX9 (Zhang and Grosse, 1997).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about DHX9 structure supported by a citation.

claim: Both N- and C-terminal regions of DHX9 bind the N-terminal FG/GLFG repeat region of Nup98.
source: As mentioned above, these regions also contribute binding surfaces for interacting proteins, and in this study we show that both N- and C-terminal regions of DHX9 bind the N-terminal FG/GLFG repeat region of Nup98 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by bead halo assay data.

claim: The C-terminal region of DHX9 contains an OB-binding fold that binds the unstructured FG/GLFG repeat region of Nup98.
source: Similarly, the C-terminal region of DHX9 contains an OB-binding fold that binds the unstructured FG/GLFG repeat region of Nup98 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by bead halo assay data and comparison to Prp43-Ntr1 interaction.

claim: The binding of Nup98 to DHX9 may impart structural features on the FG/GLFG repeat regions of Nup98 that facilitates binding to RNA.
source: We speculate that the binding of Nup98 to DHX9 may also impart structural features on the FG/GLFG repeat regions of Nup98 that facilitates binding to RNA.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on comparison to the Prp43-Ntr1 interaction.

claim: The binding of Nup98 to N- and C-terminal regions of DHX9 increases the ATPase activity of DHX9.
source: Reciprocally, the binding of Nup98 to N- and C-terminal regions of DHX9 increases the ATPase activity of DHX9 (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by ATPase assay data.

claim: Werner Syndrome helicase interacts with both N- and C-terminal regions of DHX9 to inhibit DHX9 activity.
source: For example, Werner Syndrome helicase interacts with both N- and C-terminal regions of DHX9 to inhibit DHX9 activity (Friedemann et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The catalytic subunit of DNA-dependent protein kinase (PRKDC) interacts with DHX9 and increases ATPase activity.
source: In another case, the catalytic subunit of DNA-dependent protein kinase (PRKDC) interacts with DHX9 and increases ATPase activity (Mischo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: DHX9 appears to be a more abundant protein than Nup98.
source: Given that DHX9 appears to be a more abundant protein than Nup98 (Montague et al., 2015; Schaab et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2012; Wilhelm et al., 2014), and that other DHX9 interacting partners appear to bind similar regions of DHX9 (Anderson et al., 1998; Erkizan et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2011; Nakajima et al., 1997; Pellizzoni et al., 2001b; Robb and Rana, 2007; Sadler et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2004; Tetsuka et al., 2004), we assume that Nup98 binds and regulates a subpopulation of DHX9.
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to protein abundance studies.

claim: Nup98 binds and regulates a subpopulation of DHX9.
source: Given that DHX9 appears to be a more abundant protein than Nup98 (Montague et al., 2015; Schaab et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2012; Wilhelm et al., 2014), and that other DHX9 interacting partners appear to bind similar regions of DHX9 (Anderson et al., 1998; Erkizan et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2011; Nakajima et al., 1997; Pellizzoni et al., 2001b; Robb and Rana, 2007; Sadler et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2004; Tetsuka et al., 2004), we assume that Nup98 binds and regulates a subpopulation of DHX9.
evidence: This is an inference based on protein abundance data and knowledge of DHX9 binding partners.

claim: The binding partners of DHX9 are likely key to determining the localization of DHX9, the specific mRNAs it binds, and its overall involvement in gene expression.
source: Overall, the binding partners (e.g. Nup98, Werner Syndrome helicase, and PRKDC) of DHX9 are likely key to determining the localization of DHX9, the specific mRNAs it binds, and its overall involvement in gene expression (Anderson et al., 1998; Erkizan et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2011; Nakajima et al., 1997; Pellizzoni et al., 2001b; Robb and Rana, 2007; Sadler et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2004; Tetsuka et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of DHX9 binding partners and their potential roles.

claim: At least some of the regulatory functions ascribed to Nup98 and DHX9 are performed by the Nup98-DHX9 complex.
source: We propose that at least some of the regulatory functions ascribed to these proteins are performed by the Nup98-DHX9 complex.
evidence: This is a proposal based on multiple experimental results showing that Nup98 and DHX9 interact and have interdependent functions.

claim: Of the gene loci that interact with nucleoplasmic Nup98, 70% produce transcripts that are also bound to Nup98 (p=6.14×10−215).
source: Specifically, of the gene loci that interact with nucleoplasmic Nup98, 70% produce transcripts that are also bound to Nup98 (p=6.14×10−215) and ~27% produce transcripts bound to both Nup98 and DHX9 (p=3.35×10−58).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of published datasets.

claim: Of the gene loci that interact with nucleoplasmic Nup98, ~27% produce transcripts bound to both Nup98 and DHX9 (p=3.35×10−58).
source: Specifically, of the gene loci that interact with nucleoplasmic Nup98, 70% produce transcripts that are also bound to Nup98 (p=6.14×10−215) and ~27% produce transcripts bound to both Nup98 and DHX9 (p=3.35×10−58).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of published datasets.

claim: Many of the genes showing altered expression following depletion of Nup98 or DHX9 contain a putative cAMP-response element (CRE).
source: Of note, many of the genes showing altered expression following depletion of Nup98 or DHX9 contain a putative cAMP-response element (CRE) (see Results).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: CRE regulated genes represent ~50% of the Nup98 interacting gene loci detected in Nup98-Dam-ID studies.
source: CRE regulated genes represent ~50% of the Nup98 interacting gene loci detected in Nup98-Dam-ID studies (Franks et al., 2016), and of these genes ~72% have their transcripts bound by Nup98 (p=4.2×10−205) and ~36% bound by DHX9 (p=2.3×10−5).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of published DamID data.

claim: Of CRE regulated genes that interact with Nup98, ~72% have their transcripts bound by Nup98 (p=4.2×10−205).
source: CRE regulated genes represent ~50% of the Nup98 interacting gene loci detected in Nup98-Dam-ID studies (Franks et al., 2016), and of these genes ~72% have their transcripts bound by Nup98 (p=4.2×10−205) and ~36% bound by DHX9 (p=2.3×10−5).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of published datasets.

claim: Of CRE regulated genes that interact with Nup98, ~36% have their transcripts bound by DHX9 (p=2.3×10−5).
source: CRE regulated genes represent ~50% of the Nup98 interacting gene loci detected in Nup98-Dam-ID studies (Franks et al., 2016), and of these genes ~72% have their transcripts bound by Nup98 (p=4.2×10−205) and ~36% bound by DHX9 (p=2.3×10−5).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of published datasets.

claim: Both Nup98 and DHX9 have been reported to bind to the CREB-binding protein (CBP)/p300, a transcriptional co-activator.
source: Consistent with these observations, both Nup98 and DHX9 have been reported to bind to the CREB-binding protein (CBP)/p300 (Aratani et al., 2001; Kasper et al., 1999; Nakajima et al., 1997), a transcriptional co-activator (Vo and Goodman, 2001).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Nup98 functions as a cofactor to regulate the ATPase-dependent transcriptional functions of DHX9.
source: These results are consistent with our in vitro analysis showing Nup98 can stimulate the ATPase activity of DHX9 and supports the hypothesis that Nup98 functions as a cofactor to regulate the ATPase-dependent transcriptional functions of DHX9.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by luciferase reporter assay data and ATPase assay data.

claim: Nup98 is predicted to stimulate the cellular activities of DHX9 that facilitate efficient processing and release of mRNAs from DHX9.
source: Nup98 is also predicted to stimulate the cellular activities of DHX9 that facilitate efficient processing and release of mRNAs from DHX9 (Jankowsky, 2011; Jarmoskaite and Russell, 2014).
evidence: This is a prediction based on knowledge of RNA helicase function and supported by citations.

claim: Depletion of Nup98 causes an increase in the binding of RNA to DHX9.
source: The latter idea is supported by our data showing that depletion of Nup98 causes an increase in the binding of RNA to DHX9 (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation and qPCR data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The Nup98-stimulated release of DHX9 from transcripts may be required to maintain the stable association of DHX9 with a gene locus by preventing it from leaving with the mRNA transcript.
source: It is worth noting that the Nup98-stimulated release of DHX9 from transcripts may be required to maintain the stable association of DHX9 with a gene locus by preventing it from leaving with the mRNA transcript.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that Nup98 depletion increases DHX9 binding to mRNAs and decreases DHX9 binding to gene loci.

claim: In the absence of Nup98 the occupancy of DHX9 at genes regulated by these proteins is reduced while DHX9 association with the corresponding mRNAs is increased.
source: This idea is consist with our data showing that in the absence of Nup98 the occupancy of DHX9 at genes regulated by these proteins is reduced while DHX9 association with the corresponding mRNAs is increased (Figures 9 and 10 and Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by DamID and RNA immunoprecipitation data shown in Figures 9, 10, and Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: Defects associated with disruption of the Nup98-DHX9 complex would alter splicing.
source: Given the RNA binding properties of the Nup98-DHX9 complex, and that transcription and mRNA splicing are often coupled, we envisage that defects associated with disruption of this complex would alter splicing.
evidence: This is a prediction based on knowledge of coupled transcription and splicing.

claim: The analysis of cells depleted of Nup98 or DHX9 revealed shared splicing defects at the level of E1A reporter and throughout the transcriptome.
source: This proved to be the case as the analysis of cells depleted of Nup98 or DHX9 revealed shared splicing defects at the level of E1A reporter (Figure 13) and throughout the transcriptome (see Results).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 13 and analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: These observations are the first to suggest a role for Nup98 in mRNA splicing.
source: Our observations are the first to suggest a role for Nup98 in mRNA splicing, and are consistent with a previously proposed role for DHX9 in splicing regulation in mammals (Hartmuth et al., 2002) and Drosophila (Pellizzoni et al., 2001a; Reenan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings supported by citations to previous studies on DHX9.

claim: The role for Nup98 in regulating DHX9 may extend to other DExH/D-box proteins.
source: Finally, we must make note that the role for Nup98 in regulating DHX9 may extend to other DExH/D-box proteins, since five other RNA helicases were identified as Nup98 interactors in our study, including DDX21, DDX5, DDX17, DHX15, and DDX3.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the identification of other RNA helicases as Nup98 interactors.

claim: Five other RNA helicases were identified as Nup98 interactors in this study, including DDX21, DDX5, DDX17, DHX15, and DDX3.
source: Finally, we must make note that the role for Nup98 in regulating DHX9 may extend to other DExH/D-box proteins, since five other RNA helicases were identified as Nup98 interactors in our study, including DDX21, DDX5, DDX17, DHX15, and DDX3.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data from the Nup98 immunoprecipitation.

claim: DDX5 and DDX17 are highly similar proteins that act as corepressors and coactivators through their interaction and modulation of transcription factors.
source: DDX5 and DDX17 are highly similar proteins that act as corepressors and coactivators through their interaction and modulation of transcription factors (Fuller-Pace, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Like Nup98 and DHX9, DDX21, DDX3, and DHX15 have also been implicated in the antiviral immune response by sensing viral dsRNA and contributing to the regulation of expression of interferon and interferon-stimulated genes.
source: Like Nup98 and DHX9, DDX21, DDX3, and DHX15 have also been implicated in the antiviral immune response by sensing viral dsRNA and contributing to the regulation of expression of interferon and interferon-stimulated genes (Fullam and Schröder, 2013; Lu et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: It will be important to determine whether Nup98 modulates the activity of other RNA helicases and, in this context, plays a more general role in regulating RNA processing.
source: Consequently, it will be important to determine whether Nup98 modulates the activity of these other RNA helicases and, in this context, plays a more general role in regulating RNA processing.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions based on the findings of this study.
